transcript.text: I am the operations lead at a tour company. Each month I tell our local partners how many guides to reserve in each destination for the month after next. If I reserve too few, we hire freelancers at the last minute for about three times the price; if I reserve too many, we pay a small fee for each guide we do not use. My director asked me for a machine learning model that forecasts how many bookings we will receive per destination each month. The table I shared is our booking export up to late February 2026: one row per booking with the booking date, travel date, destination, nationality, channel, lead time in days, price, whether it had free cancellation, and whether it was cancelled. I will use the result myself every month to fix the reservation. [shares bookings.csv]

Now a closer look at the pieces that decide the design.

Understood, and I can see the shape of it: you are not really forecasting bookings for their own sake — you are choosing, twice-ahead, how many guide-days to commit to in each destination, under a penalty that is about three times worse on the short side than on the long side. That last fact matters more than the model.

**One thing needs saying before any work.** The target your director wrote — "how many bookings we will receive per destination each month" — is the wrong quantity to reserve against, and building it as asked would cost you money twice over. Your export shows why: 22.8% of bookings are cancelled, so a booking forecast is roughly a quarter too high in demand terms (Dubai 25.8%, Paris 19.8%). And 67.5% of bookings are made 60 or more days before travel, median lead 92 days — so at the moment you make the call for month M+2, you have already received about two-thirds of that month's bookings in your own system. A forecast of gross monthly bookings, reserved against, both counts cancellations you will never serve and re-forecasts demand you already know exactly. The right target is **arriving travellers per destination in the travel month**, and the model's job is mostly to predict the *remaining* third plus how cancellations move. I'd build that instead.

On ~5 destinations × ~13 fully-observed travel months, a "machine learning model" must beat a plain scaling rule or it isn't worth the maintenance. I'll test it that way rather than assume it wins.

**The plan I'd run**
1. Reshape the export into a monthly demand table: per destination per travel month — bookings, arriving travellers, and arriving already in hand at the 60-day cutoff. Check: totals reconcile against the raw rows; TEST rows out.
2. Set the yardstick: a no-model rule (in-hand ÷ that destination's early-booking share, blended with last year's month shape), scored in money.
3. Fit the forecast model on destination × month with in-hand as a feature, validated walk-forward on the last 3 travel months only, scored on your cost function (3× shortfall, small fee surplus), not on average error.
4. Pick the reserve level from the asymmetry — a quantile above the mean, how far above depending on your fee.
5. Deliver it as a monthly view: in-hand, forecast, recommended guides, and the expected cost of trusting it.
Stop rule: if step 3 does not beat step 2 in money, we ship step 2 and I say so plainly.

Those are the three ways in, and I'd take them in that order rather than in the order written: **the yardstick rule first**. It does the reshaping that option 3 would do anyway, it gives you a reservation number you could act on next month, and it puts a bar on the table that a model has to clear before it is worth maintaining — which matters here, because one summer of history can't prove a seasonal pattern on its own. Then we build the forecast model against that bar, and it ships only if it wins in money.

Pick the one you want and I'll start it. If you'd rather I just decide, say so: I'd run the yardstick now and set the model up as the next step, and I'll need two figures from you whenever we get to the model — the fee you pay for a guide you don't use, and how many arriving travellers one guide covers.

(I left out the parts whose numbers I cannot source from you or your data. Ask me about any part in words and I will go through it.)

choices.title: The yardstick rule first (a week of numbers, no model)
choices.what: I rebuild the export into destination-by-travel-month demand (arriving travellers, and how many are already in hand 60 days out), then score the simple rule 'scale up what is already booked' against your real history in money. You get: A reservation number you could use next month, plus the bar the ML model has to clear, and a clear view of each destination's early-booking share and cancellation rate. Trade-off: It is not a model and will not learn new patterns (a channel shift, a price change) the way step 3 would. Effort: Small: one table build and one scored comparison, today.

choices.title: Go straight to the forecast model
choices.what: I set up a prediction project: target = arriving travellers per destination per travel month, features = destination, month, in-hand count at the cutoff, lead-time mix, channel and nationality mix, price level; walk-forward validation and a quantile output so the reservation sits above the average, as your cost asymmetry wants. You get: What your director asked for, judged on the money you would actually have saved or lost each month, plus a per-destination recommendation. Trade-off: and it needs two numbers from you (the unused-guide fee, and how many travellers one guide covers) before the reserve level means anything. Effort: Medium: build, validate, then a monthly run.

choices.title: Clean the export into a forecast-ready table
choices.what: I turn the booking rows into a tidy monthly file first: drop the 12 TEST rows, fix price as a number, derive travel month and the 60-day-cutoff in-hand counts, and check every destination's totals reconcile. You get: A single table you keep using, on which both the rule and the model can be run or re-run without re-doing the arithmetic. Trade-off: It produces no forecast itself; you would still need one of the other two after it. Effort: Small: one cleaning recipe, today.

You picked the yardstick — that is the right order, and it can hand you an April number today. Let me start it and pull the pieces.

`cancelled` is 0/1 — 1,157 arriving, 343 cancelled. Now the four views the rule needs.

Two of these numbers don't line up, and that is more important than the yardstick itself — checking before I hand you an April figure.

The mismatch has an explanation, and it changes the baseline. Re-running the shares on the months the export can actually see completely.

Both charts are up. Here is what the yardstick says, and a trap in the baseline that I found before trusting it.

The early months are thin because of the file's start date, not because business was slow. So scaling April 2026 off April 2025's 50 would have told you to reserve about a third too few guides — and that is exactly what the chart comparing "already booked for April 2026" with "April 2025 arrivals" looks like at first glance: 9 against 10 in Bangkok, 12 against 8 in Dubai, 14 against 13 in London. Ignore the year-ago column.

**April 2026, read at the 60-day position:** 9 booked in Bangkok, 11 in Dubai, 9 in Istanbul, 13 in London, 11 in Paris — 53 in hand. These are arriving bookings, not guide-days.

A revision clause at 30 days would save more on last-minute freelancers than any forecast model will, because the missing third is mostly *not yet in the world* at the moment you decide. That reframes the model's job: predict the late-booking tail, and don't oversell precision.

And one number only you have: **how many arriving travellers does one reserved guide cover in a day** — and does a booking typically mean one traveller or a family of four?

[DCLab drew a chart with its numbers table and a chart with its numbers table above this message]

Good — then I'll decide the two open numbers myself, state them, and build the yardstick so it is usable the moment you disagree with them.

Now the numbers that make the rule per-destination rather than one global average.

The per-destination shares differ more than the global average suggested. Getting the error band and the two charts the rule needs.

Recorded. Here is the yardstick, calibrated on the clean window only.

Here is the rule, and it fits on one line per destination. **The yardstick: arriving bookings = what you hold at 60 days ÷ this share**

| Destination | In hand at 60 days (clean window) | At 30 days | April in hand | April estimate | Reserve at the 75th |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bangkok | 62.1% | 78.8% | 9 | 15 | 17 |
| Dubai | 62.4% | 83.2% | 11 | 18 | 20 |
| Istanbul | 63.7% | 82.3% | 9 | 14 | 16 |
| London | 67.8% | 81.8% | 13 | 19 | 22 |

transcript.text: I am a data scientist at a company that sells accounting software to small firms. Two years ago we built a model that scores every new lead on how likely it is to become a customer, and the sales team calls the highest scores first. Since the autumn the sales team says the top leads are much worse than they used to be, and my manager wants me to retrain with a larger model and more features. Some context on the data: since the summer, part of our leads comes from a partner marketplace; we moved to a new CRM in August, and two form fields the model uses are no longer collected; and finance now counts a lead as converted when a free trial starts, where before it was the first payment. I have the old training set and every lead since, not yet exported. What would you do?

Here's what I read in your context, because the four things you listed *are* the diagnosis.

**The problem.** Your model's job is to rank leads by how likely they are to become customers, and sales works the top of that list. Since autumn the top looks worse. Retraining with a bigger model can't fix any of your four changes — three of them break the measurement itself, and the fourth breaks the training data:

1. **The target moved.** "Converted" used to be first payment, now it's trial start. Trials are far more frequent than payments, so on the new definition the model probably looks *better*, not worse — and any conversion rate you plot across autumn is two different numbers joined by a line. Training on a merged history teaches a blend of two definitions.
2. **The population moved.** Marketplace leads arrive with different intent than your own inbound. The score's cut no longer means the same thing across sources.
3. **Two features stopped existing.** This is the quiet one: whatever the serving pipeline puts in those blanks now — null, a fixed default, a stale carried-over value — the score's *range* collapses. A feature that is constant can't separate anyone, and your top decile becomes whoever the remaining features rank by accident.
4. **The loop.** Sales call the top scores first, so low-score leads are barely worked and their conversions are invisible. Retraining on that data mostly teaches the model to agree with itself. And "the top leads feel worse" may partly be an attention effect: same leads, more of them, same reps.

**What needs care before any work.** Don't retrain yet. If you do, you bake in the definition change and the selection bias, and hand your manager a larger model that beats the old one only on a metric nobody agrees on. Also don't compare months on the label as finance records it today — rebuild both label versions from raw event dates first.

**My approach:** measure, attribute, then retrain on a corrected spine — and break the loop while you're at it.

**The plan**
1. **One row per lead**, everything since the old training set: score *as issued at the time* (not recomputed), source, CRM event dates, trial start, first payment, whether and when sales contacted it. Checked by month counts and by no leads lost in the migration.
2. **Confirm the complaint is real**, on a consistent label: top-decile conversion rate by month under both definitions, plus calibration (predicted vs realised). This gives you a break date.
3. **Attribute it**: hold each suspect fixed — marketplace vs direct leads *within the same score band*; missing rate of the two dead fields over time; score distribution shift; contacted vs not. The break date lining up with August, the summer, or neither is the answer.
4. **Retrain** with the dead fields dropped and a source flag, validated on a post-August period, judged on lift@decile and calibration, not AUC.
5. **Randomise a slice** of top-scored leads for a few weeks so your future labels aren't shaped by the current model.

Stop rule: if step 2 shows no measurable drop on a consistent label, we don't retrain at all — we re-run it on revenue.

Pick one of the three above to start. If you have the export, the diagnosis is the one I'd take; the first needs no data from you. The thing that would change my plan most: when sales say the top leads are worse, do they mean fewer *paying* customers, or fewer trials that start?

## 1. The target was redefined (converted = trial start, was = first payment)

**Mechanism.** Trials are several times more frequent than payments. Under the new label the model almost certainly looks *better*; the top decile's conversion rate jumps for reasons that have nothing to do with quality. A history that mixes the two definitions teaches an ill-defined target — `p(outcome)` where outcome means one thing before the change and another after.

**The trap inside the trap — label maturity.** Payment lands weeks after the trial. If finance switched to trial-start, then your autumn months' *payment* labels are right-censored: those leads simply haven't had time to pay yet. A top-decile drop that appears exactly in recent months is the classic signature of immature labels, and no amount of model work fixes it.

**Test.** Rebuild both labels from raw event dates (trial_start, first_payment) on the whole history. Then plot the two labels separately, by month.

**Ruled out if:** the drop persists at a fixed, fully-elapsed horizon on the payment label.

## 2. The population moved (partner marketplace since summer)

**Mechanism.** Two distinct effects. Intent shift: marketplace leads trial easily and pay badly (price-shopping, self-serve), so the top decile fills with leads that look excellent on a trial label and worthless on revenue. Support shift: those leads sit in feature regions the old training set barely covered, so their scores are extrapolations — often clustered just below the old prior's ceiling. **Test.** Per month: share of the top decile that is marketplace; top-decile conversion by source and blended. A gap within band means the score is not comparable across sources and needs a source term plus per-source calibration. Compare within-source lift too: if the model ranks marketplace leads well among marketplace leads, you have a routing problem, not a model problem.

**Signature:** the break date tracks the marketplace ramp, and the drop vanishes when marketplace leads are excluded.

## 3. The feature pipeline broke (two fields stopped, new CRM)

**Mechanism, and this is the one that flattens a top decile.** If serving fills the missing fields with a constant, a mean, or a mode, those features carry no information *and* they push every post-August score toward the training mean. The score's variance collapses. Your top decile is then a tie — resolved by float noise or CRM insertion order — so it stops being the best leads and becomes an arbitrary grab from the upper-middle. Sales experiences precisely "the top leads are much worse than they used to be."

**Second mechanism:** the migration can also change surviving features' encodings — `1-10` vs `Small`, country codes, date formats, a rebuilt categorical vocabulary. Unseen levels silently become the unknown bucket.

**Test.** Per feature, per month: missing rate, unique count, mean/sd, top-category share; look for a step at the cutover. Then per month: the score's own sd, min, max, decile boundaries, and how many distinct scores sit in the top decile — variance compression is visible in one query. Then the controlled experiment: recompute scores for **pre-August** leads with those two fields replaced by the constant serving uses now. If the known-good months degrade to the autumn's observed quality, the outage explains it entirely, and no new features are needed.

**Ruled out if:** score sd and top-decile composition are unchanged after August.

**Mechanism.** Conversion is partly *caused by* contact.

Here is the decision design. Take it to management as the thing being approved — the model is a component of it, not the deliverable.

## 1. The decision, stated properly

Not "approve or decline." Three things happen at once, and the design must separate them:

- **Who** gets credit (the risk ranking)
- **On what terms** (line, term, deposit, product)
- **Under what budget** (how much loss the portfolio may carry while growing)

The rulebook collapses all three into one binary at full amount. That is why it sits at ~40% and why a like-for-like model will just rescale it — the risk the domain expert named plainly: a new model that only finds new names for the same 40%, dressed as innovation. Judge this project by *approved applicants whose expected default stays inside a break-even loss budget*, never by approval rate or accuracy.

## 2. The control: a signed loss budget, not a target approval rate

Management should sign two numbers, and only two:

- **Expected loss ceiling per vintage** — e.g. 12-month net loss on originations, in currency, agreed up front.
- **A growth cap on the unproven part** — how many incremental approvals you'll accept whose risk has no history behind it.

The approval rate is then an **output**, not a target. This matters for you personally: if the approval rate is the KPI, someone will hit it and the loss will arrive twelve months later, after the bonus conversation. If the loss budget is the KPI, the approval rate can only rise where the economics permit it.

## 3. The three decision bands

Auto-approve / refer / auto-decline, entered by predicted risk, with:

- **Auto-approve band:** above the line, no human. Reason codes logged for every decline.
- **Refer band:** a thin slice of genuinely marginal cases to your underwriters. At a shop counter this may be operationally impossible — which is itself a finding, and pushes risk into the auto-decline side.
- **Auto-decline:** plus **re-present rules**. What happens when a customer is declined and comes back next week, or at a different shop? Without a rule, you learn nothing from repeat attempts and the shop has an incentive to shop your counter.

## 4. The cutoff comes from economics, not from the ROC curve

A loan is worth approving when its expected contribution is positive. Roughly:

> approve if expected loss (default probability × loss given default) is below **margin + merchant commission − funding cost − servicing cost − required profit**

That gives a **break-even default probability**, and it is the only defensible reason to approve someone the rulebook declined. Note it's a *marginal* test, not an average one: the incremental approvals are worse than your book average by construction, so average profitability will mislead you. I can't compute it — those are your numbers, and they're the first thing missing from your export.

## 5. The levers management hasn't thought about

In POS finance, "approve more safely" rarely comes from passing more people at full line. It comes from **structuring**: a declined-at-full-line applicant may be sound at a smaller line, shorter term, with a deposit, or on the appliance rather than the phone. That converts declines into approvals at a risk you chose. It also, usually, lifts approval rate more than the model does.

## 6. Govern the swaps, don't backtest them

The interesting population is the **approve-swaps**: people the model passes and the rulebook declined. There is **no data on them and never can be** — you cannot backtest the exact group the project exists for. So:

1. **Shadow mode** first: score live traffic, decide nothing, for a few months.
2. **Controlled approve-swap pilot**: a small, random, capped share of rulebook-declines approved deliberately, with an amount cap. This is the cheapest information you will ever buy, and it is the only honest answer to "can we approve more safely."
3. Compare **rulebook survivors / model survivors / crossed approvals** as separate cohorts, always by vintage, never by point-in-time defaults.

findings.text: About 60,000 funded loans with a 12-month default flag support training only on applicants who passed the rulebook, while declined applications have no outcome.

A new model may simply rescale the rulebook's about 40 percent pass rate rather than find genuinely safe customers. Success should be measured by approved applicants whose expected default probability stays inside a break-even loss budget, not by higher approval volume or model accuracy alone.

Can the credit risk manager supply the loss budget, expected revenue contribution, cost of funds, servicing cost, recovery severity, line size, term, deposit, and product mix needed to derive a break-even default probability and cutoff?

Retail POS credit can create apparent growth from dealer-driven baskets, product categories, thin-file customers, seasonal phone launches, or repeat re-presents after a decline. Those effects can concentrate approvals in high-risk pockets without improving true portfolio risk.
How will automated declines provide adverse-action reason codes that a customer can understand, and how will the team test disparate impact when no human is between the model and the shop counter?

The swap should be governed first by shadow scoring and a controlled approve-swap pilot, separating rulebook survivors, model survivors, and crossed approvals, before replacing the rulebook at the counter.
